Aiah
ā´yah
n. (the father of Rizpah, Saul's concubine; also a Horite chief)
Hebrew Ayyah, a hawk or kite — the bird of prey named in the food laws. The name is remembered because of a daughter who kept the birds of the air off her sons' bodies.

Biblical Definition

Rizpah enters the record as a political grievance: “And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” (2 Samuel 3:7). She reappears when David hands seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites: “But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul” (2 Samuel 21:8). What she then did is one of the longest single acts of endurance in Scripture: “And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night” (2 Samuel 21:10). She sat on a rock from barley harvest until the rains — months — driving off carrion birds from the bodies of her two sons and five others. David heard of it, and it moved him to act: “And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land” (2 Samuel 21:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Aiah; the Hebrew signifies a hawk or kite, and the name belongs to the father of Rizpah and to a Horite chief.

expand to see more

AIAH, n. The father of Rizpah, concubine of Saul; in Hebrew, a hawk or kite.

CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man without the authority of a legal marriage; in Scripture, a wife of secondary rank.

SACKCLOTH, n. Cloth of which sacks are made; coarse cloth worn in mourning, distress or humiliation.

VIGIL, n. Watch; devotion performed in the customary hours of rest or sleep; a keeping awake.

INTREAT, v.t. To ask earnestly; to beseech; to supplicate; to be prevailed upon by entreaty.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 3:7 — "And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?"

2 Samuel 21:8 — "But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:"

2 Samuel 21:10 — "And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night."

2 Samuel 21:14 — "And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land."

Modern Corruption

The passage is used to indict God for the deaths, or Rizpah is sentimentalised into a symbol, and the covenant breach that caused the famine goes unmentioned.

expand to see more

The chapter is read as one of the ugliest in Scripture and is often cited as evidence of a savage God. The narrative gives a cause the complaint usually omits: a three-year famine, an enquiry of the LORD, and the answer that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Israel had sworn an oath to the Gibeonites in Joshua's day and Saul had broken it, and the land lay under the consequences of a violated covenant. Scripture is not commending the reprisal as a model; it is recording how seriously God takes a sworn word, including one obtained under false pretences.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour Scripture pays to a grief that would not be hurried. Rizpah could not undo the executions and did not try. She spread sackcloth on a rock and stayed from the beginning of barley harvest until the rains came, keeping the hawks — the very bird her father was named for — off the bodies. She had no standing, no power, and no legal claim. What she had was constancy, and it reached the king, and the dead were buried, and after that God was intreated for the land. The Bible does not tell her story in order to solve it. It tells it because she was there.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Ayyah (H345), a hawk or kite; pilegesh (H6370), a concubine; saq (H8242), sackcloth; athar (H6279), to be intreated.

expand to see more

Hebrew Ayyah (H345) — a hawk, kite; the father of Rizpah, and a Horite chief.

Hebrew Ritspah (H7532) — Rizpah, meaning a hot stone or coal.

Hebrew pilegesh (H6370) — a concubine, a wife of secondary rank.

Hebrew saq (H8242) — sackcloth; what she spread upon the rock.

Hebrew athar (H6279) — to entreat, be entreated; God was intreated for the land.

Usage

"“Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah” — named four times by her father."

"“From the beginning of harvest until water dropped” — the length of the vigil."

"“After that God was intreated for the land” — how the chapter ends."
